utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Are we ready now to proceed with the witness? Thank you. Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, yesterday the Defence worked on intensively going through the documents, and all we can say is that we've managed to go through most of the documents that were given to us, not all of them. In order to avoid wasting your precious time, we think we should just proceed. The Defence has no problem continuing the -- or rather, starting the examination-in-chief of Witness Jokic now. We do, however, have to point out the following: If we consider the material we received in terms of its content, we will certainly be using the CDs during our cross-examination because they contain everything that we've been trying to underline about the nature of those materials over the last couple of days, even without the transcripts, even without video material. The Defence will be in no position to conduct its cross-examination in a proper way. Therefore, I would like to ask the Honourable Chamber to assist the Defence in this respect, to help us to obtain copies of the transcripts of this video material and to have the cross-examination postponed until these further materials are served on the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. Rodic, inquiries that have been made by the Chamber indicate first, of course, that it is not simply a matter of obtaining copies of the transcripts. There are no transcripts. It is a matter of effecting a transcription of the material you have. That involves two stages; first a change of the electronic form in which it is held to a form suitable for transcribing and then the process of transcribing. That, we are told, involves in the order of double the length of time of the total running length of the tapes that you have. Not only is it a lengthy process, but there are no people available at the present to do that work. They are already committed with other work that has been previously allocated and is needed. Therefore, there would seem to be no realistic prospect of having a transcript of all of that material available to you at the time for cross-examination. So that the Chamber must ask you to prepare your cross-examination as best you can, knowing of that material but not being in a position of having a transcript as you do cross-examine. Now, you may well be able to find some way, in discussion with Ms. Somers, of making that a reasonably speedy and practical process. I do not know. But the alternative would seem to involve a very considerable delay in the trial. Given the nature of this material, the Chamber therefore must ask you to press on with what we appreciate will be a difficult and inconvenient process, but one which I hope with your cooperation and, if necessary, that of the Prosecution, will prove to be practical.

utterances.speaker: MR. RODIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. But what I wanted to say is: May the Defence please be helped, assisted, in a timely manner. Possibly after Witness Jokic there will be another witness, and even if these transcripts cannot be made, we would still be needing quite a lot of time to go through these documents, CDs, again and take out whatever we need from them. It will be very difficult for us to handle these during our cross-examination. For example, if the question is asked: Where specifically did the witness state this? All I can say in terms of a reference is the third CD dated, for example, the 17th of February. That's the best reference I would be able to give. In order for me to provide even that sort of a reference, the Defence should have to keep notes in terms of something resembling a transcript, which is a very time-consuming activity, in addition to which there is plenty of other material related to Witness Jokic. We will have great difficulty in this effort. Therefore, if we may just be given another bit of time between the two examinations when a new witness comes along, or rather, before a new witness comes along, to give additional time to the Defence team to go through the material for our cross-examination, we are able to make a great effort to master this material and be able to conduct our cross-examination in a proper manner.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Mr. -- I see Ms. Somers on her feet. She may be in a position to offer some help, so I will listen to what it is she wishes to say.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you, but it was not in respect of the cassettes or the tapes. Yesterday the Prosecution indicated that if at the end of the planned cross-examination the Defence were to make an application for additional time, that we don't know what the substance of it would be, but certainly we would not oppose the making of an application and we would seek a request to respond. In terms of the scheduling of witnesses, we have planned the order of witnesses so that immediately after the cross-examination of Admiral Jokic, we have another witness scheduled. But reworking the witness schedule would probably be somewhat difficult and we think that the Chamber has been very fair in its apportionment of time to review items that may or may not have been helpful but -- and we appreciate it and would ask simply that we proceed as planned, and should, at the end of the initial cross-examination, there be an indication of a need, then again we would not oppose the making of an application, and depending on the grounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you for your comments, Ms. Somers. There are some disadvantages in what you propose. In particular, it means that the first cross-examination by the Defence may be less effective than they would wish because they have only part of the material ready that may be relevant to a point of cross-examination. And another obvious difficulty is that it really requires, to some extent at least, a second going over of the same ground, so that it is an undesirable and inefficient approach. The Chamber, while not absolutely closing the door on it if it proves to be the only possible way forward, would prefer that there be a serious exploration of alternatives to try and overcome this difficulty that has arisen. At the end of the examination-in-chief, I take it from what you say the Prosecution will not be in a position to have another witness that could be interpolated at that point.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: We think it would be difficult to get this witness. We can certainly make the inquiry. If the Chamber will allow us the opportunity, we would be very happy to try to do that but otherwise proceeding as the Chamber indicated, and that would be as much as I could interpose at this time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, if you could do that and explore the possibility, we'll, I think, need to leave the question open at least until the end of cross-examination -- end of examination-in-chief. But if you could explore the possibility of there being another witness available. If that is not possible, it may be necessary to have yet another day or two's break to enable the Defence to be in a position to adequately cross-examination on the whole case.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: As the Chamber sees fit. We will -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: That, we think, would be in the long run more efficient than twice cross-examining over the ground. Could we also invite both counsel to explore constructively the best way of enabling some ready reference. One thought that occurs to me as I speak is the possibility that if the Defence were able to provide a note informally to the Prosecution of the passages that they can see they will be referring to, it will enable the Prosecution at least to have identified those passages in advance and so speed up the process of reference and cross-examination. But there may be other means, and we leave that to your constructive discussion. So, Mr. Rodic, at the moment, as I have indicated, the Chamber would prefer and will expect that you will proceed to cross-examine the witness. It may be necessary for there to be a short delay after the end of the witness's evidence in chief before you commence. The possibility of another witness being interposed before your cross-examination will be explored. If that is possible, it may help. But I think at the moment you must prepare as best you can to cross-examine not only with the original two statements of the witness available to you, but with the record -- the tapes of these new discussions of the witness in the form that they are. And anything you and Ms. Somers can work out to make that process speedier and more practical I think will help us all. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can -- pursuant to your directive, if I can ask the Defence if there are specific numbers on any particular CD. In other words, give us a number reference and we'll see if we can assist. With that degree of specificity, we're happy to try to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Well, if we could now have the witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Prosecution calls Admiral Miodrag Jokic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Good morning. Would you be kind enough to take the card that is to be placed in front of you, and if you would take the affirmation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. If you could please be seated. Yes, Ms. Somers. Examined by Ms. Somers:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Good morning, Admiral Jokic.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you please state your full name.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: My name is Miodrag Jokic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And your date and place of birth, sir.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: I was born on the 25th of February, 1935, in Mionica near Valjevo in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And by ethnicity, what are you, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: I am a Serb.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you to give us an overview of your educational background, and if you could start, for example, as far back as 1954 and take us forward to your -- all the way through your military academic training.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: I completed my secondary education in Valjevo in 1954, after which I joined the naval academy in Divulje near Split. I graduated three years later in 1957, after which I started boarding patrol ships and torpedo ships, rocket-carrying ships. I completed two specialised courses, artillery, rocket, and torpedo specialisation courses, specialised courses, between 1964 and 1966 I completed the higher naval academy. In 1976 I graduated from the School of National Defence --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, in what year -- have we gone up to 1966, is that where you're at now? If you could just take us back to the year. 1966, which academy?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Between 1964 and 1966 I attended and completed -- graduated from the higher naval academy.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And after your graduation, Admiral, did you start having assignments?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes. After the academy I was assigned to the Split destroyer, where I stayed until the year of 1970, after which I spent three years on new torpedo boats. I was the division commander on those boats, after which I became the commander of a rocket brigade. In 1975 I was sent for further schooling at the School for National Defence in Belgrade. Having graduated in 1976, I was assigned to the Boka Naval Sector. At the command, where I was first the chief of operations and then the chief of staff, in 1980 I was sent back to Belgrade to the general staff to work as the chief of the naval development section. In 1983, I was returned to the Boka Naval Sector to work there as sector commander. I stayed there for five years, until 1988. In 1988, I was again sent back to Belgrade to pursue a course in All People's Defence. I remained, however, in my previous position, but I was sent for further education. In 1989, having completed that course, I was back in my sector. In December I was sent back to Belgrade --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "sent back to my sector," which sector are you referring to, sir?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: The 9th Boka Sector. In 1989, in December, I was again sent to Belgrade, to the Secretariat for National Defence of Serbia to work there as secretary, which was to all practical intents an appointment with the Serbian government. I stayed there for one and a half years. Towards the end of July 1991, after the government had been restructured, I was left out of the government and I was sent back. I remained unassigned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, quick question about a position that you indicated you held that you referred to as Secretariat for National Defence of Serbia, serving as secretary. Is that also a title which might be called Minister of Defence at the republican level?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes. The first five months the government was working under President Stanko Radmilovic. It was a transitional government. And the name of the ministry was the Secretariat for Defence, the Defence Secretariat, which was a republican ministry which all the republics in the former Yugoslavia had. Six months later, following the elections, a new government was formed, and the sector was renamed as the Defence Ministry and I became Defence Minister in the Zelenovic government.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral Jokic, I have a question about whether or not you had any specialised courses in artillery. If you did, could you describe them.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: I had completed a specialised course for artillery and rockets in Pula, 1961 and 1962. Before I started boarding torpedo ships, I had attended a specialised course like that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral Jokic, when did you complete your service as Minister of Defence for the Republic of Serbia?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: I was left out of the government on the 31st of July, once the government had been restructured, the Zelenovic government, and I was replaced by General Simovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there a period of time after you left your position as Minister of Defence when you were not working in either the government or actively in the military?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Once I was out of the government, I was left without an assignment. I no longer worked with the army, so I went back to the village in which I had been born. I was greatly dissatisfied with my current status, so I looked after my father's garden on his farm.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time of your retirement, what rank had you achieved?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Vice-admiral. I had been promoted to the rank of vice-admiral in 1990, on the 22nd of December. That was Army Day.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you retire from the forces we refer to as the JNA? When did you retire?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: I left the JNA in May 1992. I believe it was on the 8th of May specifically, that's when I retired.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you actually leave your service, or was that a paper date?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: That's when I was relieved of my duties as commander of the 9th Naval Sector. In practical terms, I think I left service altogether in August, several months later. But the decision on retirement and for me to be relieved of all my duties occurred on the 8th of May, 1992.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any significance to the date 21st of May, 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Not that I know of.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: After your break from being Minister of Defence of Serbia, did you find yourself reassigned to another military position?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: No. I was not reassigned. I lost my position. I had the status of an officer without assignment, but I was not assigned another position or duty. I was dissatisfied by the sort of treatment I was meted out and therefore I left Belgrade and went back to my native village. I had no other duties to the army.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Were you reassigned at some point to the 9th Naval Sector in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the 6th. On the 5th in the evening, I received a telephone call while I was in my village --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, 5th of what month, Admiral?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: The 5th of October in the evening, I received a phone call from Belgrade to report to the general staff and see General Adzic. It must have been the secretary, personal assistant, calling. I was supposed to report by 12.00 the following day, on the 6th. I went to Belgrade --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know why you were supposed to report?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: To report to duty. That's what I was told. And that as soon as I got there, he and General Kadijevic would inform me about the details. This happened in the evening, I think it was at about 11.00. Speaking to me on the phone was a personal assistant who either was not aware of exactly why I had to go or was reluctant to tell me. The next day, I travelled to Belgrade and reported to General Adzic at about 12.00. He asked me if I had my equipment with me, if I was able to start right off. He said I would leave with General Kadijevic at 5.00 in the afternoon, that I should go and speak to him --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What did he tell you to do? Leave for where?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: He told me that I would leave for Boka to take up my duties as the commander of the 9th Naval Sector. Admiral Djurevic, he said, had been killed. His helicopter had been taken down and he said that I would now become the commander of that sector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know when Admiral Djurevic was killed? Do you have an approximate date?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: He was killed on the 5th in the afternoon, around 1500 hours. I learned this later, of course, how and why, and so on and so forth, once I had arrived in Boka.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Admiral Djurevic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did know him from the navy. He was a submarine officer. He was a signalsman. He was on submarines all the time, whereas I was on ships for 18 years. And I think that he spent quite a few years in submarines, and later on he was transferred to the headquarters of the navy -- or rather, of the naval sector in Split.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, do you -- if you know, do you know what ethnicity Admiral Djurevic was?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: He was Montenegrin from Danilovgrad.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At what point, Admiral, did you take over his, that is Admiral Djurevic's, post at commander of the 9th Naval Sector? What date?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: I came during the night between the 6th and the 7th -- or rather, the 7th around 10.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Or rather, 2.00 a.m., interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I came to Kumbor, Herceg-Novi. I came to the command on the morning of the 7th. The then acting chief of staff, Captain Zec, welcomed me and familiarised me with the situation, briefed me. Then I met Ruzinovski, who was commander of the 2nd Operations Group and who came to the command at Kumbor when I was assuming my duty. Then the situation was totally unknown to me: The troops, how they were grouped, the actual situation in the theatre of war, because in Serbia, as I stayed in the country, I could only read about the beginning of the Dubrovnik operation in the newspapers and hear about it over the radio and on television. On the 8th, I think that I was practically appointed. This was this order that I didn't even have at the time. The date was the 8th of October. On the 8th of October, in the afternoon, Admiral Djurevic was buried in the town of Kotor. I delivered a speech at his funeral, and many others did, too. In the meantime, I toured the battlefield, and if you ask me when in effect I took over the command, perhaps it can be put this way: As of the 9th, there are orders bearing my signature. Although everything was calm on the front line, there was no need for combat orders in terms of the operation itself, because on the 8th, the 8th of October, there had been a cease-fire.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you, Admiral. I'm going to try to ask you to perhaps respond a bit more briefly, and we appreciate the completeness of your answers. A question about your -- the -- you said: "I only could read about the beginning of the Dubrovnik operation." Was it your understanding that you were coming to the 9th VPS, or naval sector, in relation to the Dubrovnik operation?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, you mentioned a commander named Ruzinovski. Can you tell us, please, his ethnic background, if you know it.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Milad Ruzinovski was a Macedonian.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned Commander Ruzinovski in connection with the 2nd Operational Group. Did you report to General Ruzinovski?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I assumed my duty and when I started commanding my units, I was subordinated to him. I did report to him, and I also did everything else that he required.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was his command -- what did he command, what formation?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: He was commander of the 2nd Operations Group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is an operational group, Admiral Jokic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: An operational group is a formation, a command formation, at the level of an army. That is to say corps are underneath it. Specifically, this was a new command, a newly established command, the 2nd Operational Group. It did not exist before. It became necessary to carry out such a broad operation like the Dubrovnik operation, and therefore it became necessary to establish this kind of group. It consisted of three corps, because this is the 9th Naval Sector and the 2nd Tactical Group. In the beginning, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you able to indicate the purpose behind this type of formation, an operational group?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Well, the purpose is to carry out a certain operation. If an army -- if a corps from the point of view of formation is not in a position to carry out successfully a certain operation within a part of the front line or the entire front line, then for the purpose of that kind of operation a new command is established, like the 2nd Operational Group. Units are subordinated to it, and these are the units that are to carry out the mentioned operation. At that time in the area of Yugoslavia, we had the 1st Operational Group and the 2nd Operational Group, as far as I can remember now.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If you know, do you know when the 2nd Operational Group was formed, if you are able to articulate it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: The 2nd Operational Group was formed sometime in September, mid-September, in Eastern Herzegovina near the town of Nevesinje. Kifimo Selo was the first place where the headquarters were. It was formed from the manpower of the main inspectorate of the Yugoslav People's Army and partly personnel from Belgrade, or rather Podgorica, I think.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In the 2nd Operational Group were there forces from only land or forces from only naval -- or were there naval forces, land forces; both? Can you describe the composition of the forces.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: In the 2nd Operational Group, there were mainly land forces, JNA units, Territorial Defence units. And within the 9th Sector, which is a mixed command anyway, there were naval forces, too. The 2nd Operational Group did not have any air force of its own, but it did have the support of the 97th Air Force Brigade. And parts of this brigade did act on orders of the commander of the 2nd Operational Group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral Jokic, at the time you assumed your duties in October of 1991, was a naval blockade of Dubrovnik already in effect or in place? Is there perhaps a translation problem?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's all right now. Yes. Yes. Before the 1st of October, the 30th of September it was, that's when a naval blockade of Dubrovnik was ordered in order to prevent the arming of Dubrovnik. It was carried out on the basis of a UN resolution, I think, in order to stop arms smuggling into the Yugoslav republics.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral Jokic, how long did you serve under Commander Ruzinovski? What period of time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: I served until the 13th of October; from the 8th until the 13th of October.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And then what happened to Commander Ruzinovski?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Ruzinovski was withdrawn to Belgrade. He was appointed to a different position, and General Strugar was appointed to his position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say "General Strugar," the first name of General Strugar, if you know it, please.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: General Pavle Strugar. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, you mentioned that the chief of staff of the operation group was a Captain Zec. Had you had occasion to work with Captain Zec before being reassigned in October of 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: No. Captain Zec was acting chief of staff in my sector, not in the 2nd Operational Group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you know Captain Zec from prior times?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. Yes, I knew Captain Zec at the time -- from the time when I commanded the sector. When I commanded the sector, he was chief of operations and he also held some other duties. After the death of Admiral Djurevic, he was appointed acting commander. For a few days, he was acting commander until I arrived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you describe some of the functions and duties that constituted General Strugar's role as commander of the 2nd Operational Group.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Well, these duties are prescribed in our combat rules, the rules and regulations of service in the JNA, and other combat rules regulating the duties of the commander at such a level. An army commander, practically. He was given tasks from the general staff, and he carried out these tasks through his subordinate units, those that were within the forces he commanded.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what was his authority to direct and command operations?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: He had full authority in relation to the objective that the operation had. And these objectives of the operation he carried out on the basis of the tasks that he was given every day by the general staff. The initial document by which the Dubrovnik operation started was the directive that was written just before the operation started, just before the 1st of October. It regulated all the objectives of that operation and the tasks of the units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was your understanding of who in the 2nd Operational Group's zone of operations, what was your understanding of who had the highest level of military authority?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Its commander, the commander of the 2nd Operational Group, General Pavle Strugar, was the man who had the greatest authority. He commanded all the units within this 2nd Operational Group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you refer to General Pavle Strugar, are you referring to the individual who is the accused in these proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you, Admiral, to look at a document which is --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Tab 1, Your Honours and counsel, in the binder that has been provided.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This document refers to -- this is the document which shows the structure of the units of the 2nd Operational Group from the 7th of October, 1991, when I assumed the duty of commander of the 9th Sector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you have anything to do with the preparation of this document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I made this document. And it exactly corresponds to the truth -- or rather, it fully coincides with the structure that was established at the beginning of the Dubrovnik operations, the structure of the command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, if you can take a look at it. First of all, did you give this document to representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Looking at the top of the document, you have the date of 7 October, 1991. Then in sort of an organigramme, it's 2OG, 2nd Operational Group. And who is listed at the 7th of October as the -- at the top or the head of the 2nd Operational Group?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: General Ruzinovski, General Mile Ruzinovski.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, immediately below the 2nd Operational Group box, you have five boxes. Can you explain, please, what the relationship of the units in those five boxes is -- was as of that date to the 2nd Operational Group and what are the units.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes. These are the subordinate units of the 2nd Operational Group. I can read them out from the left going to the right. The first one is the 37th Corps; then the 2nd Corps; then the 9th Military Naval Sector, my command, my unit; then the 472nd Motorised Brigade; and finally, the 2nd Tactical Group. Those are the first commands that are subordinate to the command of the 2nd Operational Group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As you see them, Admiral, are they directly subordinated at that time to the 2nd Operational Group?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, directly.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can I ask you, please, Admiral, the commands of the corps -- the commands of the various formations are listed underneath. If you could be good enough to read 37th Corps, et cetera, so that we know who was commanding at the time.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes. The commander of the 37th Corps or the Uzice Corps as it was called because that's where its headquarters were before, was General Milan Torbica. The commander of the 2nd Corps or the Podgorica Corps was General Dragutin Eremija. The commander -- or rather, the acting commander of the 9th Military Naval Sector Boka was, at that time on the 7th of October, Captain Milan Zec, and I took over from him. Then the 472nd Motorised Brigade, or the Trebinje Brigade because its headquarters were in the town of Trebinje in Herzegovina, the commander was Colonel Obrad Vicic. And the 2nd Tactical Group, which was a newly established unit which carried out duties in Konavle, and the commander was General Stankovic, General Branko Stankovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, when you indicated Captain Zec as the, I believe you said acting -- I'm sorry, that you took over from him. Was he there in between Djurevic and yourself?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. During those two or three days.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And as chief of staff, what is his relationship to the formation for which he is chief of staff if the commander becomes unavailable through death or substantial absence in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: The chief of staff is the deputy commander. He stands in for the commander in any situation when the commander cannot carry out his duties or when he is not present. He is also in charge of the command staff. That is his specific duty.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, I note that among various formations, including corps and the VPS tactical groups, there is a brigade that is directly subordinated to the command or the commander of the 2nd Operational Group. What -- can you tell us something about the 472nd Motorised Brigade. Did it have any other name? Was it known by any other name?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes. The 472nd Motorised Brigade was also referred to as the Trebinje Brigade. It used to be part of the 9th Military Naval Sector of Boka before. Several years earlier, when I was still the commander, it was part of its composition, however, prior to the commencement of the Dubrovnik operation, four or five days earlier, the general staff singled this unit out from the Boka sector and resubordinated it to be part of the 2nd Operational Group, directly resubordinated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral Jokic, what is your understanding of why a brigade was subordinated on par or the same level, as it were, with corps, this particular brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: I can't know for certain what the reasons were, but as commander of that level I can speculate about the reasons that the general staff may have had. The unit had about 6.000 people. It was a strong unit. It was a strike force that was to be focused on the main objective of the Dubrovnik operation, which was the blockade of the town of Dubrovnik. The way it was first conceived - I saw documents testifying to this - was that the 9th naval district should not take part in Dubrovnik operation, but rather only the brigade. However, this was later changed, probably because the sea was involved and that there would be tasks on the sea. This was the sort of environment that the operation was being carried out in and commanders of land forces were probably less well-equipped to carry out tasks in that sort of environment.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Admiral, when you say: "It was a strong unit," which unit are you referring to? You said: "It was a strong unit."

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the Trebinje Brigade, the motorised brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The 472nd?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely, 472nd.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, what is a strike force, or your understanding of a strike force?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes. A strike force is the force which is the agent of a certain objective, of a certain task, focusing on defence or offensive operations in a particular operation, in a particular assignment. So this is the key unit, in other words, for the success of a mission, the mainstay of a mission. And this unit is usually referred to as a strike force.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral Jokic, within the 2nd Operational Group, was there an intact chain of command?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes. The command of the 2nd Operational Group was structured according to the rules governing the structuring of a command staff. It had the fundamental organs that enabled it to control combat operations for units of this size. It was a newly established unit, but it did have chiefs of branches and services who prepared the unit for combat operations, who drafted the unit's documents. And it was on the basis of these documents that they monitored and ran the combat operations of their subordinated units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Within "documents," Admiral, do you include orders?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, I'd like to ask you to take a look now at an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: In tab 2, Your Honours, in the binder. Your Honours, I'm sorry. My colleague reminds me, as to the document at tab 1, the Prosecution would ask that it be tendered into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: What is the practical course that you foresee with this binder? Should that be treated as one exhibit in the end or --

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: No, sir. We put it together for your convenience so you have them easily tabbed, but we will go document by document. And some have already been, in fact, in evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, then the document at tab 1 will be received as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Prosecution Exhibit P99.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, if you have in front of you now a document which bears the number -- our number in the corner of 03520418, that's the evidence number. The date on this document is the 6th of December, 1991. Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And how do you recognise it? Why do you recognise it?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: I wrote this document myself. This document is about the structure of the units subordinated to the 2nd Operational Group on the 6th of December, 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you turn this document over to representatives of the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, now looking at your chart organigramme giving the structure of the 2nd Operational Group as of the 6th of December, 1991, at the top where it says 2nd Operational Group, or 2OG, whose name is now in the command position?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: The commander of the operational group was General Pavle Strugar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you take us through, please, the formations which were at that time directly subordinated to the 2nd Operational Group.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: At that time there was the 37th Corps, the 2nd Corps, and the 9th Military Naval Sector.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, looking at the 9th Military Naval Sector, or VPS which is how we will refer to it during the course of your testimony, are there now subordinate units; and if so, can you please identify them for us?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes. On the 6th of December, under the 9th Sector, there were the following units: The 3rd Battalion of the 5th Motorised Brigade, the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Motorised Brigade, the 3rd Light Brigade, the Trebinje Territorial Defence branch and the corresponding battalion, as well as some territorial units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm asking my colleague Ms. McCreath if it's possible to put the first chart you had next to this one on your computerised evidence. If it is possible, it might take a second. Admiral, do you have both of your charts in front of you on the screen now?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can see that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Will you please summarise then the differences, the changes, in the formations that are shown; what units may have remained or what units may have left.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Well, the difference between these two charts consists in the following: The 472nd Motorised Brigade became part of the 2nd Corps. It was no longer directly subordinated to the 2nd Operational Group. The 2nd Tactical Group had been disbanded and no longer existed as an operational unit. The units that were under the 2nd Tactical Group, those two brigades, had been resubordinated to other establishments. As of the 2nd of October, it ceased to exist as a command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, you have indicated that the 472nd or Trebinje Brigade became part of the 2nd Corps. However, it appears from your chart that a battalion from the 472nd Brigade has remained and is subordinated to the 9th VPS. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes. The 3rd Battalion was separated from the brigade and resubordinated directly to the command of the 9th Sector. Without it, the brigade left the Dubrovnik area and was resubordinated to the 2nd Corps in order to carry out other tasks.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What type of battalion was the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd? What was your understanding of its value to have it remain in the 9th VPS and not go with the rest of the battalions of the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: All the battalions of the Trebinje Brigade, establishment-wise, were the same. This battalion was assigned to become part of the 9th Sector because there was a need for a unit like that to be deployed around Dubrovnik in order to block Dubrovnik from the south and the south-east from the direction of Trebinje.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The commander, the commanding officer, as of the date of the 6th of December of the 3rd Battalion, the 472nd Brigade, was who?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Colonel Obrad Vicic was the commander.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm sorry, of the 3rd Battalion, Admiral, of the 472nd.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: The commander of the 3rd Battalion of the Trebinje Brigade was Captain Vladimir Kovacevic, who had taken up his duty after the previous commander of that battalion had been seriously wounded. That was Major Ekrem Devlic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did Captain Kovacevic go under any other name or nickname?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes. The nickname was Rambo.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A question about the 472nd Motorised Brigade staff officer or chief of staff: Who was that individual, the chief of staff of the 472nd Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Komar. I think his name was Major Miroslav Komar. He was the chief of staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Komar. And was he the chief of staff from the time you re-entered the 9th VPS until at least through the 6th of December?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. For the whole time. He was deputy brigade commander, in that position.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I will move on to another document, but I would ask that the document from tab 2 be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P100.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Turning your attention now, Your Honours, to the document which is in tab number 3.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral Jokic, do you have the document in front of you or are you able to take a look at it, please?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document, Admiral?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for counsel, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm terribly sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This is a combat order, number 6, of the command of the 9th VPS. This order was written at my command.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And does it bear your name?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the date of the order?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: The date is the 20th of November, 1991, 1700 hours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To whom is it addressed?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: This is an order addressed to the -- to my subordinate units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And is there a reference to the 2nd Operational Group there, Admiral Jokic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes. This document, being a combat order, was delivered to my subordinate units and to the 2nd Operational Group, to the attention of the 2nd Operational Group since the 2nd Operational Group was my superior command in this case.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The first paragraph, Admiral, addresses itself to the 472nd Motorised Brigade, but it says without the 3rd Battalion. Can you indicate why --

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Without the 3rd Battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, how many battalions were there in the 472nd Motorised Brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Four.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So for 1, 2, and 4, why is the 3rd Battalion exempted from this particular command? And perhaps you might be good enough to tell us what the order is designed to do.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: The purpose of this order, first of all, under 1 it says: "Pursuant to the decision of the Commander of the 2nd OG strictly confidential number," and so on and so forth, "to further action, leave the complement of the 9th VPS and work on orders from the 2nd OG," and the 3rd Battalion will be left with the 9th VPS. I think that's the overall meaning of the order, for the brigade to leave, the 9th VPS, the composition of the 9th VPS, and for the 3rd Battalion to be temporarily resubordinated to the 9th VPS.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, does it then go into specifics about the -- about various aspects of obligations of various subunits and various formations within the 9th VPS?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, what was the purpose of leaving the 3rd Battalion within the 9th VPS and moving out the other three battalions to another formation?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Well, the main purpose was that a decision had been made at the level of the 2nd Operational Group for the 472nd Brigade, which was no longer needed in the blockade of Dubrovnik because the main objectives had been reached, and this brigade was needed elsewhere in Popovo Polje and even further afield. As for the needs of the 9th Sector, it only took one battalion, the kind of the 3rd Battalion, in order to be deployed in positions around Dubrovnik and to secure that the blockade of the town continued.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know the approximate number of units of strength of the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd at that time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Establishment-wise, the battalion numbered about 700 people. I'm talking about these motorised units. There were four companies. Its composition, three were motorised, or rather, infantry companies, and one was anti-tank company. And it also had a mortar battery. It numbered a total of about 700 men.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you tell us, please, the history of the decision to move the other battalions out of the 9th VPS and -- I'm sorry, the other battalions of the 472nd out of the command of the 9th VPS, and were they removed from the immediate area?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Once the objectives had been achieved to set up a blockade of Dubrovnik in late October, the commander of the operational group ordered a meeting to be held on the 2nd of November in Trebinje at his command post. At this meeting, decisions had to be reached regarding further deployment of forces and further operations. Having in mind the fact that the Trebinje Brigade was a very large and strong unit with a great manpower and that it was no longer necessary to keep it in the surroundings of the town, especially on account of the frequent provocations, frequent firing, there were a large number of men there who had nothing to do. So my proposal was, as on a previous occasion, for this brigade to be moved out of the area surrounding Dubrovnik, and the group commander accepted this proposal, the tactical group command -- the operational group commander accepted this proposal. This was to be done on the 6th of November

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Excuse me, Admiral. It was a bit of a choppy sentence: The operational group commander accepted this proposal. Who are you referring to when you say operational group commander?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: I mean General Strugar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, let me ask you, please, from what period of time did you have the entire brigade as part of the 9th VPS?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: This brigade was part of the sector as of the 26th of October and was to remain there until the 6th of November. That's according to all the combat documents that we had. However, due to a change in the circumstances, it stayed there until as long as the 21st of November.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, you were -- you were telling us when I asked you an additional question. You said: "So my proposal was, as on a previous occasion, for this brigade to be moved out of the area surrounding Dubrovnik, and the group commander, tactical group -- operational group commander accepted this proposal." And you began to say: "It was to be done," and then you didn't finish, and I apologise. If you could finish what you were going to say.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: It was to be carried out on the 6th of November. And all the units that had to replace this brigade had reached their destinations. The 3rd Battalion of the 5th Motorised Brigade, the Territorial Defence Battalion from Trebinje, and the Territorial Defence detachment from Trebinje were to replace this brigade. However, this order to relieve the brigade, to withdraw the brigade and send it to Popovo Polje and further afield, this order was never carried out. Therefore at that time I had twice as many units as had originally been there in my operational zone; those who were there to replace the brigade and the brigade itself which never left.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Is that a convenient time, Ms. Somers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Yes, it is, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: We will now have a 20-minute break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Somers.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to ask -- excuse me. I would like to ask that the last document from tab 3 be moved into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P101, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, I would like to go back for a moment to something you said on page 28, line 13, of the transcript, which was: "Having in mind the fact that the Trebinje Brigade was a very large and strong unit with a great manpower and that it was no longer necessary to keep it in the surroundings of the town, especially on account of the frequent provocations, frequent firing." I want to ask you: What was your principal concern about the Trebinje Brigade? You mentioned that on previous occasions you had discussed or you had indicated it should be removed. What was your concern?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: What I bore in mind was the following: There was no longer any military necessity for such a strong unit to remain in the surroundings of the town. Because it was rather difficult to keep so many troops there under control, especially if the units are not active, if they do not receive tasks, then it is only natural for the troops to create problems.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, when you say, Admiral: "For such a strong unit to remain in the surroundings of the town," which town are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: I mean the town of Dubrovnik.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You have just indicated that if they do not receive tasks, it is only natural for the troops to create problems. What kind of problems are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: I was referring to unnecessary opening of fire, because it was a fact that discipline was not at the required level. Units consisted, for the most part, of reservists, in most places even over 50 per cent. Also, on the other hand, Croatian paramilitary formations were also carrying out provocations. Because in their smaller units there were personnel who were extremists, too, and then they were involved in provocations as well. So these provocations coming from both sides create a situation that is hard for commanders to keep under control.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral Jokic, when you use the term "Croatian paramilitary formation," are you using it to mean the defence forces of the Croatian side or your opponents?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The brigade, I believe you indicated, was a strong brigade heavy with manpower. Can you please describe the type of weaponry that the various battalions of the brigade had.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: The composition was the same. They had three infantry companies, or rather, motorised companies; they had one anti-armour company that had 82-millimetre mortars; it had recoilless guns, hand-held launchers, rocket launchers, too, Maljutkas. In order to give artillery support, or rather, to have artillery support, each battalion had mortar support of 120-millimetre mortars.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Perhaps at a later point, Admiral, we'll ask you to discuss in detail the numbers of weapons, but at this point in time the types of weapons are helpful for us to know. You have indicated that discipline was not at the required level in the brigade. Can you please elaborate on that.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: This brigade previously had been one of the best trained units in the entire Yugoslav People's Army. It was the brigade of the navy infantry that had been mobilised from that area, Herzegovina, Montenegro, the Croatian coast, and Dubrovnik. However, after the situation that came to be due to the internal conflict between the Croatian paramilitaries and JNA units, the brigade was rather quickly mobilised, and it was only personnel from Herzegovina and partly from Montenegro who were mobilised. So it was not the regular type of mobilisation. It wasn't the kind of soldiers like the brigade used to consist of before. Many of them were not properly trained, and some of them were even volunteers, people who had volunteered into this brigade. So part of the personnel was undisciplined and insufficiently trained for use in such combat situations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And was this a situation you found with the brigade when you first returned to the Dubrovnik theatre -- I'm sorry, when you first returned to the command of the 9th VPS, was this the situation you found or learned of with the brigade?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, precisely.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You had indicated that on a previous occasion you had proposed the withdrawal of the brigade. Can you discuss the occasion and what the underlying reasons for your proposal for withdrawing it were.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: No. I bore in mind another unit. When I came to the Dubrovnik front line on the 7th of October and as I was touring Konavle between Dubravka, Cilipi, all the way up to Cavtat, the units that were there, I saw many troops belonging to another unit of the 2nd Tactical Group that had major forces in a narrow area like in this brigade. There weren't any real objectives. There was no military necessity, no military need involved, and especially there was no need for such strong artillery. I suggested to the commander of the 2nd Operational Group, General Strugar, that a brigade be taken out of this 2nd Operational Group because it was not required for further action. This unit was commanded by General Branko Stankovic. That's when the first brigade was drawn out, the Partisan Brigade of the Territorial Defence, as its official name was, because there was problems with discipline, with unauthorised shooting, and also some looting and arson.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, which Territorial Defence are you referring to, which unit?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: I was referring to the newly established 2nd Tactical Group that operated in Konavle from the outset of the Dubrovnik operation. It consisted of two brigades of the Territorial Defence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The Territorial Defence of which republic are you referring to, Admiral Jokic?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: The Republic of Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe you referred to: "There was no need for such strong artillery." Can you please indicate what you mean by "strong artillery." How did you see the composition of the artillery in the units you're referring to, and did you view it perhaps as excessive?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I think -- or rather, I should say first and foremost that the general assessment was that our units of the Yugoslav People's Army, according to their establishment, were organised in such a way and trained in such a way in order to be in a position to act against an aggressor, a strong enemy. So that is why they had this strong artillery. However, bearing in mind the fact that our opponent was not a strong army against whom one needed to use such strong artillery and such equipment, in this situation when we were acting against poorly armed paramilitary forces, such artillery often got in the way, especially in Konavle, especially in built-up areas where there were no proper targets. These were 130-millimetre guns, and also guns and Howitzers of 122 millimetres, and mortars and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, who had the 130-millimetre guns et cetera? Which units are you saying had them? In other words, are you referring to the JNA units?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. These are units -- there were two batteries, one of 130 millimetres, the other one of 85 millimetres. And these two batteries were resubordinated at first, and also there were Howitzers of 120 millimetres. And the 472nd Brigade had the strongest artillery; it had two such divisions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Just to clarify, Admiral, when you said: "In this situation when we were acting against poorly armed paramilitary forces," are you referring to the Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Petrovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I'm sorry. Admiral Jokic, in his response to the previous question, said exactly where each artillery unit was. However, unfortunately, I cannot see it reflected in the transcript. So could Admiral Jokic please clarify exactly where which unit was. All of us heard it here, all of us who are present here heard him say that. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Do you wish to clear up the matter, Ms. Somers?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I would just ask if I can get the point I was asking for clarification on first and then return to my learned friend's question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you said or referred to "against poorly armed paramilitary forces," are these forces -- again, are you referring to the Croatian forces?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I was referring to.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, perhaps we can assist Mr. Petrovic in understanding your response that he suggested is not in the transcript. And if the question is -- let's see. Clarify exactly where each unit was when you referred to: "These are our units, there were two batteries of 130s." If you're able to do that at this point.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: The 9th Sector had two artillery units, one battery of 130 millimetres and one battery of 85 millimetres, both of them mobile. At the beginning of the Dubrovnik operation, these units were outside the operational zone, across the Bay of Boka at the peninsula of Ljustica. As the operation developed, these batteries were transferred across the bay, and I think between the 3rd and 5th of October, they were resubordinated to the 2nd Tactical Group, which was the protagonist of all the main activities in the field of Konavle. In addition to that, this 2nd Tactical Group had artillery of its own, that is a battery of 122-millimetre [as interpreted] equipment, and it had mortars. Every brigade had 120-millimetre mortars. This was a respectable artillery force. I mean, all of this was happening before General Strugar assumed his duties in the 2nd Operational Group.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification. The organisational chart that you had looked at, Admiral, for the 6th of December -- rather, the one you had discussed with us, also discusses a subordination of other battalions; the 3rd of the 5th. Can you indicate, please, who is the commander of the 3rd of the 5th and describe that particular formation. First of all, what is the 5th, and talk about that particular battalion.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: It's not the 5th Battalion; it's the 3rd Battalion of the 5th Brigade. That's probably what you meant.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for correcting me, Admiral.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: The 3rd Battalion of the 5th Brigade was at the beginning of the combat operations within the 2nd Tactical Group. It was a battalion that was from the 5th Motorised Brigade from Podgorica. So it was taken out of this 5th Motorised Brigade in Podgorica and resubordinated to the 2nd Tactical Group. When the 2nd Tactical Group was disbanded on the 21st of October, this battalion was directly resubordinated to me. And it operated all the way up to the end of December within the 9th Sector as a temporarily resubordinated unit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, who was its commander?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Its commander was Major Srboljub Zdravkovic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Continue, please. You were telling us more.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: The 5th -- that battalion of the 5th Brigade had the same kind of composition like the 3rd Battalion of the Trebinje Brigade. However, in the beginning when the operations started in Konavle, it had within it a company of obsolete tanks from the Second World War and it also had a company of armoured carriers. Later on, when it was resubordinated to me, these APCs were taken out of this unit and were sent to another unit, I don't know exactly which one, but outside of my area of responsibility anyway.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Ms. Somers, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We have put back on the screen, if it might be of assistance to you, the formations you indicated for the 6th of December. It should be in the Sanction screen, I believe it's up, your computer screen. And if you could briefly describe the other units by their abbreviations. It would be helpful to know what the abbreviations stand for and a little bit about the units, please.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: I've already said that the 3rd Battalion of the Trebinje Brigade, which was commanded by Captain Vladimir Kovacevic, I've already spoken about the composition of that battalion.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. There are other abbreviations: "Tc," "3rd," "3rd lbr."

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes, the 3rd Light Brigade is a weak unit. It was established in haste. It consisted of five companies, altogether 12 to 1300 men, partly volunteers, and their artillery was weak. Therefore, this unit did not have any particular combat value. It was primarily used for tasks in auxiliary directions and in control of territories. As for the Territorial Defence of Trebinje and the battalions of the Territorial Defence of Trebinje, these were classical territorial units that did not participate in combat operations. They only controlled the territory, had guard duty, and so on. These territorial companies were small units, infantry units. They had small arms, primarily from these municipalities along the coast of Montenegro, Herceg-Novi, Kotor, Tivat, Budrat [phoen], Bar, and some other municipalities from Montenegro, like Mojkevac and Bijelo Polje and so on. These are units that did not take part in the attack either. They were used for controlling the territory, for guarding facilities, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In which republic is Trebinje, Admiral?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Trebinje is in Bosnia-Herzegovina, actually in the part of Bosnia-Herzegovina which is called Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Until what point in time was the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade under the 9th VPS?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: This battalion became part of the 9th VPS on the 10th of November, 1991, and it remained within the sector all the way up to the end, the 31st of December, and perhaps even a bit later. While I was commander, that is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If -- perhaps you could clarify, was it equally part of the Trebinje Brigade of the 472nd which you indicated came under your command sometime at the end of October? Just a yes or no would help.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, the changes you just spoke about -- let me just cite for a moment. Excuse me. The changes in subordination of units or formations that you have discussed, between the 7th of October on your one document and the 6th of December, who effected or who brought about those changes which you have described? Upon whose order?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: This is the order of the commander of the 2nd Operational Group. In his system of command, he asked his subordinate commands and his subordinate commanders to give their own proposals, proposals on how the units could be used in the most rational way. On the basis of these proposals as to how the units could be used in the best possible way, he reached decisions on resubordination, re-establishment, and so on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Then after the 12th or 13th of October, when you refer to the commander of the 2nd Operational Group, you are referring to whom?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: General Strugar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'd like to ask that you turn your attention to the document under tab 4.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: The Prosecution acknowledges that the date of the document is in early 1992, and the purpose of reference is not necessarily of the substance, but rather of the person whose order it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, this document is dated the 5th of February, 1992, a period outside of this indictment, but who is the person whose name is appearing at the bottom of this document?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: That's the commander of the 2nd Operational Group, General Pavle Strugar.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: To whom is this particular document addressed?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: This particular document is addressed to the first administration of the general staff.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And what is the nature of the document? What type of information or what is the content of this document?

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: We apologise that we have not been able to provide yet a translation. We have requested it and we will submit it as soon as is possible; therefore, I have to ask the Admiral to discuss the document.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In this document, at the request of the first administration of the general staff, the composition of the units of the 2nd Operational Group is submitted in relation to the JNA units, the TO units, and the volunteer units.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And in the paragraph which would be -- if you don't mind for a moment, in order to assist the Judges who do not have an English translation, if you would be helpful and perhaps read it through. A quick exercise, but if you could do it, it would be helpful. Where it says -- I'm sorry, Admiral, I mean if you could read it to us out loud.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: In the document reference is made to the units that comprise the structure of the 2nd Operational Group. The first reference is made to the 2nd Corps, and then it says: "The units of the JNA," within this 2nd Corps, that is, and then they are listed. Since this is the 5th of February, 1992, this is the Trebinje Brigade, the 472nd Brigade, and then artillery units. The Howitzer division, 122 millimetres, a battery of multi-barrelled rocket launchers, 326, and then the TO units are listed. These were first the JNA units then come the TO units. That's the Partisan Brigade of the TO, Sava Kovacevic, then the volunteer units, the 1st Light Brigade and the 2nd Light Brigade.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the second page of the document there's a reference to VPS Boka.

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: These are your units?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes. These are my units. And this is where the composition is referred to, which JNA units these are. And all establishment units of the 9th Sector are listed here. Practically, they did not take part in the Dubrovnik operation; they did not take active part in it. As for those that were attached, those that were resubordinated to me temporarily, reference is made to the 3rd Battalion of the 472nd Brigade. And then there is a mistake. It is not the 1st Battalion of the 5th Brigade but it is the 3rd Battalion of the Motorised Brigade. Those are units of the JNA. So these two battalions are within my composition; they were resubordinated to me. As for the TO units, reference is made to the TO Trebinje Battalion. As for the volunteer units, reference is made to the 3rd Light Brigade that I spoke of awhile ago.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Admiral, did you continue to remain subordinated to the command of the 2nd Operational Group at this time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did all -- were all the units mentioned in this document subordinated to the 2nd Operational Group at this time?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And the commander of the 2nd Operational Group at that time continued to be General Strugar?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. SOMERS
utterances.text: I'm going to ask to move this document into evidence, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: It will be received.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Prosecution Exhibit P102.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Going back, Admiral, to the issues of indiscipline or lack of discipline within the 472nd Motorised Brigade, what was the nature of the indiscipline and was it apparent when you came into your command?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: It was obvious. It would have been obvious for any commander, any professional commander, who exercised command over any troops. This lack of discipline was manifested in noncompliance with orders or a poor level of compliance with orders, mutual grudge between individuals, extreme forms of behaviour, uncontrolled use of weapons, mutual firing and wounding, the consumption of alcohol by certain individuals, individual instances of looting, arson. There were also instances of acts of provocations being carried out by firearms, by artillery provocation against the other side or fire being returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. PETROVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we have an interpretation problem. I'm sorry. The interpretation says that acts of provocation by artillery were carried out. I believe the general said infantry fire provocation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PARKER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Petrovic. That will be corrected.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In response to what you've described as apparent indiscipline, what, if any, suggestions or proposals did you make to the commander of the 2nd Operational Group?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: The commander of the 2nd Operational Group in his orders, on a daily basis usually, as is apparent, that most energetic measures be taken to prevent lack of discipline. The subordinated commands did so; some more and some less successfully. However, it was very difficult to altogether put a stop to these incidents. Problems were considerable and the conditions under which operations were being carried out were not favourable for the exercise of any form of command. For example, it was considered that the units were taking part in a military drill, and then a decision was made that 45 days later all units should be sent home for leave, as this decision also comprised units throughout the entire state. And then the units requested leave 45 days later to go home and get some rest. However, the commands were not able to ensure this. Moreover, since the state of war had not been declared, there was difficulty in applying war regulations sanctioning these instances where lack of discipline was manifested. There were very few military police and it was also for this reason that it was difficult to punish each individual act of indiscipline. So this is a pattern that was repeated over time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And were attempts or orders to implement discipline adhered to by those to whom the orders were issued or did there continue to be disciplinary problems?

utterances.speaker: MIODRAG JOKIC
utterances.text: The commands made a great effort to deal with these problems. We had one or two seminars, we had daily meetings, we had military collective meetings.
